problem: Standard encoder-decoder attention for translating natural language navigation instructions into behavior plans computes attention only from the current decoder state, ignoring useful patterns in earlier attention and introducing translation errors.
motivation: Indoor robots lack GPS, so natural language is a practical way to give navigation commands. Accurately translating instructions into executable behavioral plans requires better use of alignment information across decoding steps.
key_idea: Add an attention-history reader network that captures patterns in the sequence of past attention distributions and uses them when generating the current attention.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations are visible. The abstract suggests that conditioning attention on its own history reduces translation errors relative to standard attention, but it gives no specifics.
method: Base model: encoder-decoder with attention that translates navigation instructions into behavior plans (behavioral navigation graph style).
Attention-history reader network: reads the history of previous attention distributions to extract patterns.
History-conditioned attention: the current attention is computed from both the decoder state and the attention-history features.

setting.backbone: encoder-decoder seq2seq with attention-history reader (trained from scratch, presumably RNN-based)
setting.training_data: Stanford Navigation Dataset (instruction to behavior plan pairs)
setting.action_space: sequence of behavioral navigation plan tokens (high-level behaviors)

results: The abstract states the method achieves higher scores than the traditional attention model on the Stanford Navigation Datasets. No numbers were given.
limitations: Evaluated only on the Stanford Navigation Dataset as text translation, not in embodied navigation
